guideTitle: 6 Best Smart Plugs With Energy Monitoring in 2026
metaTitle: Best Smart Plugs With Energy Monitoring 2026
metaDescription: Six smart plugs that report how much power a device uses, compared on Matter support, app charts and bill estimates for anyone watching their energy use.
introParagraphs: An energy monitoring smart plug does everything a normal plug does and then adds a meter. It switches a lamp, heater-free appliance or electronics cluster on a schedule, and it also reports how much power the connected device draws and how that adds up over days and weeks. That turns a vague suspicion about an old space fan or an always-on entertainment center into a number you can read in an app.

The value depends on the app as much as the hardware. Some plugs show clear charts and an estimated bill, while others give you a live wattage reading and little else. Matter plugs bring cross-platform control, but energy data often does not pass through Matter, so you may still need the brand app to see consumption.

We evaluated six plugs based on product specs and buyer feedback, comparing monitoring depth, platform support and extra features such as charging cutoffs. The lineup covers two Tapo models, a Matter Tapo, two Kasa plugs, a Govee model and the Emporia.

products.name: Tapo P110M Matter Smart Plug
products.description:
The Tapo P110M combines the cross-platform benefits of Matter with a built-in energy meter. Matter certification means it can work with major smart home platforms regardless of brand, which suits a household that does not want to be tied to one assistant. The energy side offers in-depth statistics and clear visuals so you can see how much a device uses.

The billing feature is what makes the numbers practical. The listing describes integration with billing systems for a clear cost view, both for a single period and over repeated periods. That helps you answer questions such as whether the older fan or the entertainment center is the bigger drain. The trade-off is that the richest energy detail will typically live in the Tapo app, rather than inside Apple Home or Google Home.

Compared with the Tapo P115, the P110M adds Matter, so it is the better pick if you use more than one platform. Compared with the Kasa Matter Smart Plug KP125, it is a close rival, with Tapo emphasizing billing views and Kasa emphasizing a long-running app. We rank it first because it offers the broadest platform support alongside meaningful energy charts.
products.bestFor: Households that want Matter flexibility and a clear view of what devices cost to run.
pros: Matter certification works across major platforms
Energy statistics and clear visual charts in the app
Bill estimate view turns watts into running cost
15A rating covers common plug-in devices
cons: Full energy data usually needs the Tapo app
Matter setup takes a few more steps

products.name: Kasa Matter Smart Plug KP125

specList.label: Platforms
specList.value: Apple Home, Alexa, Google Home, SmartThings

products.description:
The Kasa KP125 is Kasa's answer to the Matter plug with energy monitoring. It works with Matter-certified platforms including Apple Home, Amazon Alexa, Google Home and Samsung SmartThings, and it carries a 15A and 1800W maximum rating. The energy feature tracks usage over time so you can see consumption patterns and make informed choices about connected devices.

Like other Matter plugs, it keeps working smoothly across devices on your local network even when your home internet goes down. That makes it a good fit for a plug that controls something you rely on daily, such as a lamp or a fan. The printed 1800W figure also gives you a clear threshold when you check the label on an appliance.

Against the Tapo P110M, the Kasa KP125 relies on a mature app while the Tapo leans on billing views. Against the older Kasa KP115, this model adds Matter, so it works with more than Alexa and Google voice. It is a strong pick for a household that already likes the Kasa app and wants to future-proof. Check that the energy information you want is available in the Kasa app, since Matter itself often does not carry it.
products.bestFor: Kasa fans who want Matter support and usage tracking in one plug.

Usage tracked over time to show patterns
Printed 15A and 1800W limit is easy to check
Local control continues if the internet drops
cons: Detailed energy figures live in the Kasa app

products.name: Tapo P115 Energy Monitoring Plug
products.description:
The Tapo P115 is the Wi-Fi monitoring plug in the Tapo family, aimed at people who care about energy numbers more than Matter. It tracks the plug's energy use with easy-to-understand statistics and intuitive charts. A bill estimate feature integrates with billing systems to show cost, whether for a single period or repeated ones.

The feature that sets it apart is smart charging. It can automatically cut power when a connected device reaches the low-battery limit you set, which the listing frames as a way to prevent overcharging. That is useful for a charger or a battery-powered device that sits on the plug overnight. It is a practical add-on, but it depends on how that device behaves, so test it with something you can easily monitor.

Compared with the Tapo P110M, the P115 lacks Matter, so it is tied more tightly to the Tapo app and the assistants it supports. Compared with the Kasa Smart Plug Mini KP115, the Tapo adds the charging cutoff and clearer billing views. If you want the monitoring benefits without paying for Matter, this is the better value choice. It suits households committed to one voice assistant.
products.bestFor: People who want energy charts, cost estimates and a charging cutoff without Matter.

Bill estimate view shows running cost
Smart charging cuts power at a set battery limit
15A rating handles lamps, fans and electronics
cons: Not a Matter plug, so platform choice is narrower

products.name: Govee Smart Plug With Energy Monitoring
products.description:
The Govee monitoring plug reports real-time power, current and voltage in the Govee Home app. Seeing all three readings gives you more detail than a single wattage number, which helps if you want to understand how a device behaves when it starts or idles. Connecting by Wi-Fi and Bluetooth lets you reach the plug even when you are near it and the network is acting up.

The four-pack format suits a home with several devices to measure, and voice control works through Alexa and Google Assistant. You can leave a plug on the TV cluster, one on a space-hungry fan and one on a coffee maker, then compare them in a single app. The caveat is that this plug does not use Matter, so it stays within the Govee Home app and its supported assistants.

Compared with the Tapo P115, the Govee shows more raw electrical data but less emphasis on billing views. Compared with the Emporia, it comes as a multi-pack and leans on Bluetooth for setup. It is a good choice if you like to see the numbers rather than a cost estimate. For most people that depth is nice to have, but not essential.
products.bestFor: People who want to see power, current and voltage across several devices.
pros: Reports power, current and voltage in real time
Wi-Fi plus Bluetooth for easier access
Four plugs let you compare several devices
Voice control with Alexa and Google Assistant
cons: Not a Matter plug, so the Govee app is required
Raw readings are less friendly than a cost view

products.name: Kasa Smart Plug Mini KP115
products.description:
The Kasa Smart Plug Mini KP115 is the straightforward Wi-Fi monitoring plug in Kasa's range. It works with Alexa and Google Home, supports app control from anywhere, and requires 2.4GHz Wi-Fi for setup. The monitoring is part of the model name and sits alongside the usual on and off controls.

Setup is described as plug in, open the Kasa app and follow the instructions, which is a gentle experience if you have not used a smart plug before. The app handles scheduling as well as monitoring, so a single screen shows both the schedule and what the device has used. It is a dependable plug for a household that wants to watch a lamp, fan or small electronic without learning a new platform.

The limitation is that it is the older style of plug without Matter, so the Kasa Matter Smart Plug KP125 is the better long-term pick for mixed households. Compared with the Tapo P115, it offers fewer extras such as charging cutoffs. Its strength is a calm, well-known app that many buyers already trust. For single-ecosystem homes that is enough.
products.bestFor: Beginners who want a familiar app and basic energy readings.

products.name: Emporia Smart Plug
products.description:
The Emporia Smart Plug is a 15A Wi-Fi outlet that controls lights, fans, lamps, humidifiers and other appliances that plug into 120V outlets. It works with Alexa and Google Home, and it includes built-in on and off scheduling for automatic switching. The listing positions it as a way to stay on top of the energy your devices and appliances use and cut down on waste.

It is a solid choice if you want a plug that looks beyond one device. Emporia is known for energy products, so its plugs fit a household that is thinking about its overall power use. The weak point of the listing is that it gives fewer technical details than the Tapo or Kasa plugs, so check the box for exact figures.

Compared with the Govee monitoring plug, the Emporia comes with an energy-focused brand identity and a simpler feature description. Compared with the Tapo P110M, it does not advertise Matter. It suits a person who prefers a company focused on energy rather than a general smart home brand. For many that focus is the deciding point.

buyingCriteria.explanation: Some plugs show a single wattage reading while others report power, current and voltage. The Govee Smart Plug With Energy Monitoring reports all three in real time, which helps you understand startup surges. The Tapo P115 Energy Monitoring Plug and Tapo P110M Matter Smart Plug add charts and cost views on top. Decide whether you want raw electrical detail or an easy summary.

Matter lets a plug work across Apple Home, Alexa and Google Home, but energy data often does not pass through Matter. The Tapo P110M Matter Smart Plug and Kasa Matter Smart Plug KP125 are the Matter options here, and both usually show consumption in their own brand app. If you want cross-platform control, choose Matter. If energy numbers matter most, check what the brand app displays.

A watt figure means little until you convert it to cost. The Tapo P115 and Tapo P110M both describe estimated bill views that cover a single period and repeated periods. The Kasa Smart Plug Mini KP115 focuses on usage tracking without that emphasis on cost. If you want to know whether a device is worth leaving on, favor a plug that shows cost.

buyingCriteria.criterion: Load rating and what you plug in
buyingCriteria.explanation: Most North American smart plugs are rated for 15A, and the Kasa Matter Smart Plug KP125 prints 15A and 1800W max. That covers lamps, fans, electronics and similar devices. Avoid heat-producing loads such as space heaters unless the rating clearly covers them. Check the label on both the plug and the appliance before connecting.

Some plugs add features beyond monitoring. The Tapo P115 includes a smart charging cutoff that cuts power when a device reaches a battery limit you set. The Emporia Smart Plug and Govee Smart Plug With Energy Monitoring add schedules and voice control. Choose the extras that match your routine rather than paying for ones you will not use.

Almost every monitoring plug connects only to a 2.4GHz network, and a phone on 5GHz can break setup. The Kasa Smart Plug Mini KP115 states the 2.4GHz requirement, and the Govee plug uses Bluetooth to assist pairing. If you struggle with Wi-Fi settings, a plug with Bluetooth help may reduce frustration. Plan to run setup with your phone on the 2.4GHz network.

howWeEvaluated.title: Monitoring depth
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared what each plug actually reports. The Govee Smart Plug With Energy Monitoring leads on raw readings with power, current and voltage, while the Tapo plugs lead on charts and cost views. The Kasa plugs track usage over time through their app.

howWeEvaluated.title: Platform support
howWeEvaluated.description: This category looked at Matter and voice assistant coverage. The Tapo P110M Matter Smart Plug and Kasa Matter Smart Plug KP125 offer cross-platform support, while the Tapo P115, Kasa KP115, Govee and Emporia plugs rely on Alexa and Google voice. Broader support earned higher scores.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cost clarity
howWeEvaluated.description: A good monitoring plug should help you see what a device costs to run. The Tapo P115 and P110M describe billing integration for cost views over single and repeated periods. Plugs that only report usage scored lower on clarity.

howWeEvaluated.title: Extra features
howWeEvaluated.description: We noted features such as the Tapo P115 smart charging cutoff, the Emporia built-in scheduling and the Govee four-pack. Extras that solve real problems added to the score. Features that were hard to find in the product details counted for less.

howWeEvaluated.title: Setup and app experience
howWeEvaluated.description: The lineup is positioned by app maturity, with the Kasa Smart Plug Mini KP115 leading on familiarity and the Tapo plugs leading on billing views. We also looked at whether setup uses Bluetooth help or a guided flow. Buyer feedback about app stability informed the final scores.

faq.q: Does an energy monitoring plug save electricity by itself?
faq.a: No, it only measures and reports use. The savings come from what you do with the information, such as unplugging a device that draws power while idle. Schedules and auto-off timers on plugs like the Emporia Smart Plug can help. Use the data to decide where to change habits.

faq.q: Can I see energy data inside Apple Home or Google Home?
faq.a: Often not. Matter plugs such as the Tapo P110M Matter Smart Plug and Kasa Matter Smart Plug KP125 control well across platforms, but energy figures usually stay in the brand app. Plan to use the Tapo or Kasa app for consumption details. This is a Matter limitation, not a fault of the plug.

faq.q: What is the plug rating and why does it matter?
faq.a: Most North American smart plugs are rated for 15A, and the Kasa KP125 prints 1800W as its maximum. Check the label on your appliance and keep the load under the plug rating. Avoid heat-producing devices such as space heaters. Overloading a plug is a safety risk.

The product details we reviewed do not state accuracy figures, so treat the readings as helpful estimates rather than lab measurements. They are good for comparing devices and spotting large drains. For billing decisions, use them as a guide. Compare against your utility bill over time.

faq.q: Do I need a hub for these plugs?
faq.a: None of these plugs are described as needing a hub for basic Wi-Fi use. Matter plugs may need a compatible hub or controller on your platform for some features. The Tapo P110M Matter Smart Plug and Kasa KP125 are both Matter-certified. Check your platform requirements before you buy.

faq.q: What happens if the internet goes down?
faq.a: Wi-Fi plugs that depend on the cloud lose remote control until service returns. Matter plugs can keep local control on your network. Energy history in the app may pause during the outage. Manual switching and local schedules vary by model.

faq.q: Can I use a monitoring plug on a refrigerator?
faq.a: It is better not to. Cutting power by mistake could spoil food, and compressor surges can strain a plug. If you only want to watch usage, a plug with a clear 15A rating may work, but check the appliance label first. Lamps, fans and electronics are safer targets.
